title: From heartbeat to tissue fluid: integrated review
summary: Work through valve timing, cardiac output, vessel resistance and lymphatic return.
objectives: Explain answers before opening the check
takeaways: Trace cause and effect rather than matching isolated words.
Use the chapter lessons to repair missed concepts.

steps.title: Pressure determines the valve state
steps.text:
During isovolumetric contraction, ventricular pressure rises after AV closure but before semilunar opening. During isovolumetric relaxation, pressure falls after semilunar closure but before AV opening. Both phases have all valves closed; one raises pressure and the other lowers it.

Connect S1 to AV closure and S2 to semilunar closure. Electrical activation precedes the resulting mechanical action.

check.q: How can both isovolumetric phases have closed valves?
check.a: Ventricular pressure lies between atrial and arterial pressure in both; it is rising in contraction and falling in relaxation.

steps.title: Calculate before interpreting
steps.text:
For EDV 130 mL, ESV 60 mL and HR 80/min: SV = 130 − 60 = 70 mL/beat, then CO = 70 × 80 = 5600 mL/min = 5.6 L/min. Ejection fraction is SV/EDV, about 54% in this example.

Keep units with every term. Cardiac output is volume per minute; ejection fraction is a proportion, not a volume.

check.q: What happens to SV if ESV rises to 80 mL while EDV stays 130 mL?
check.a: SV falls to 50 mL/beat; at 80/min, CO is 4.0 L/min.

steps.title: Radius controls resistance strongly
steps.text:
For the idealized Poiseuille model, flow is proportional to pressure difference and the fourth power of radius, and inversely proportional to viscosity and length. Halving radius increases resistance sixteenfold if the other terms are unchanged.

Total capillary area is large because many vessels run in parallel. That explains slow average velocity without implying that one capillary has a huge diameter.

check.q: At fixed pressure difference, what happens to idealized flow when radius halves?

steps.title: Vessel leak and lymphatic return
steps.text:
Higher capillary hydrostatic pressure favors filtration; plasma proteins oppose it through oncotic effects. Increased permeability or impaired lymph drainage can increase tissue fluid.

The course’s traditional 30/27/3 L budget connects capillary exchange to lymph formation. Lymph nodes sample lymph; the spleen samples blood.

check.q: Why can a blocked lymphatic pathway cause edema even if the heart still pumps?
check.a: Fluid entering tissue cannot be returned effectively through lymphatic drainage.

practice.q: EDV 125 mL, ESV 55 mL and HR 70/min give CO of…
practice.why: SV is 70 mL; multiplying by 70/min gives 4900 mL/min.

practice.q: At fixed pressure gradient, doubling idealized radius changes flow by…
practice.why: The radius term is raised to the fourth power.
Falling ventricular pressure produces semilunar closure and S2.

practice.q: Why can left-heart failure cause pulmonary edema?
practice.a: Inadequate left-heart output raises upstream pulmonary venous and capillary pressure, favoring filtration.

title: From a tissue infection to immune memory: integrated review
summary: Connect lymph drainage, innate recruitment, antigen presentation and adaptive effectors.
objectives: Explain answers before opening the check
takeaways: Trace cause and effect rather than matching isolated words.
Use the chapter lessons to repair missed concepts.

steps.title: Locate the first filter
steps.text: Material from a left-hand wound travels in lymph toward regional nodes, then larger vessels and trunks. The left upper limb ultimately drains through the thoracic-duct territory. The right lymphatic duct drains the upper-right territory, not the entire right half.

check.q: Does left-arm lymph drain through the right lymphatic duct?
check.a: No. It belongs to thoracic-duct territory.

steps.title: Recruit and present
steps.text: Inflammatory mediators recruit phagocytes. An APC processes extracellular material and displays peptide with MHC II. A matching helper T cell recognizes it and receives costimulatory signals before expansion.

check.q: What does B7-CD28 add to peptide-MHC recognition?

steps.title: Choose the effector by target location
steps.text: Antibody can neutralize extracellular toxin or virus, coat targets for phagocytosis and recruit complement. A cytotoxic T cell recognizes an infected cell through peptide-MHC I and can induce death. Helper cells coordinate; regulatory cells restrain.

check.q: Which arm removes a cell already producing viral protein?

steps.title: Explain the next encounter
steps.text: Memory B and T cells persist after the initial response. A later matching exposure can recruit them quickly. Receiving someone else’s antibody is different: it supplies temporary protection without, by itself, establishing your own memory.

check.q: Why is maternal antibody passive even when it protects effectively?
check.a: The infant receives antibody produced by the mother rather than generating it through its own response.

practice.q: An extracellular peptide displayed to helper T cells uses…
practice.why: APCs present ingested peptides through MHC II.
Lymph passes through nodes; spleen filters blood.
Protection is transferred rather than actively generated.

practice.q: Name an innate and an adaptive killing lymphocyte.
practice.a: NK cell is innate; cytotoxic T cell is adaptive.
